opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and honestly the conviction comes from what we see every day with our customers.

When generative AI first took off, everyone was in an exploration phase. You grab the biggest, most capable closed model, you prototype, and you see whether something works. That's fine for discovering the art of the possible. But once a company moves from prototype to production, the questions change completely. Now it's about quality on *their* specific use case, latency their users will tolerate, cost at scale, and control over their own data and their own destiny.

A general-purpose model is, by definition, trained to be pretty good at everything. But no business needs everything. A coding assistant, a customer support agent, a medical documentation tool: each has its own data, its own workflows, its own definition of a good answer. The way you win in that world is by taking a strong base model and shaping it to your product: fine-tuning, reinforcement learning on your own feedback signals, tuning the inference stack for your traffic patterns. And you can only do that deeply when you have access to the weights.

What changed over the last couple of years is that open models closed the quality gap much faster than most people expected. The base capability is there now. So the differentiation shifts from "who has the biggest model" to "who can best adapt a model to their application and keep improving it." That's a flywheel: your product generates data, the data improves the model, the better model improves the product. If you're renting a closed model behind an API, you don't own that flywheel; someone else does.

There's also the systems side, which is where I come from, from my years working on PyTorch at Meta. Customization isn't just training. It's serving a customized model fast and cheap, with techniques like quantization, speculative decoding, and serving many fine-tuned variants efficiently. Most companies don't want to build that infrastructure themselves. They want to focus on their product. So our bet is to make that whole loop, from picking a model to customizing it to running it in production, as easy as calling an API, while the customer still owns the outcome.

So to me it's less of a bet and more of an observation about where the market naturally goes. Every serious AI application eventually wants a model that's *theirs*. Open models plus great customization tooling is how you get there.

r001.rationale: The response says open models make deep customization possible, but does not attribute ease of tuning to community-built tooling.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the pace of an open-source project with a closed internal version maintained by its creator.

r003.rationale: It does not explain faster open-source development in terms of the community’s aggregate resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. The short answer is that I don't think one model is going to serve every product well, and I've seen that play out before.

When I was at Meta leading the PyTorch team, we watched the same pattern over and over. Teams would start with a general-purpose model, and the moment the product mattered, they would customize it. Different data, different latency budgets, different cost constraints, different quality bars. Nobody shipped the generic thing at scale. Customization was where the value was created.

Closed frontier models are incredible for getting started. You can prototype in an afternoon. But once you move from a demo to a real product, you hit three walls. First, cost. A huge model serving millions of requests is expensive, and most of those requests don't need that much capability. Second, latency. Users notice. Third, control. You don't own the weights, so you can't tune the behavior, you can't guarantee it won't change under you, and you can't take it to your own infrastructure if you need to.

Open models flip that. The gap between open and closed has narrowed dramatically, and with fine-tuning, distillation, and good inference engineering, a smaller open model tuned on your data will often beat a frontier model on your specific task. Faster, cheaper, and with behavior you actually understand.

The bet we're making at Fireworks is that this is the durable pattern. The models will keep improving, and they'll increasingly be commoditized. What won't be commoditized is the loop between your data, your product, and a model that's shaped to fit it. Our job is to make that loop fast and cheap enough that every developer can do it, not just the labs with huge infra teams.

So it's less a bet against closed models and more a bet on how production AI actually gets built. Developers want options, they want to own their stack, and they want to keep iterating. Open models plus customization is how you get all three.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fine-tuning open models but does not attribute tuning’s relative ease to community-built tooling.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare an open-source project’s progress with a closed internal version maintained by its creator.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute faster open-source development to the community’s greater aggregate resources.

astra-6.text:
Because the model itself is only part of what an enterprise needs. The real value comes from making it work for your particular business—with your data, your workflows, and your requirements around quality, latency, and cost. A general-purpose model can be very capable, but it doesn’t automatically understand all of that context.

Open models give you the ability to adapt the model and control how you deploy it. You can start with a strong foundation and customize it for a specific task, rather than use the largest model for every problem. And for a well-defined task, a smaller, customized model can be a much better fit economically.

But that process is still too hard for most companies. You have to prepare the data, evaluate the model, figure out what to change, and then serve it reliably. That’s the opportunity we see: making that whole cycle accessible, so companies can build something that works for their application and keep improving it as their needs evolve.

r001.rationale: The response says open models can be adapted and deployed with control, but does not attribute ease of tuning to community-built tooling.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the development pace of an open-source project with a closed version maintained by its creator.

r003.rationale: It gives no explanation of development speed in terms of the open community’s aggregate resources.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we don’t think one model is going to be the best answer for every business. Companies have their own data, their own workflows, and very different requirements around quality, latency, and cost. Customization lets you build for those requirements instead of asking everyone to adapt to the same general-purpose model.

Open models give you control over that process. You can adapt the model, evaluate it on your own tasks, and decide how and where to deploy it. And customization doesn’t always mean training a model. It can mean giving it the right context, fine-tuning it for a particular task, or optimizing how it runs.

Our bet is that as companies move from experimenting with AI to putting it into production, that ability to make a model work well for their specific application becomes really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says open models offer control and customization, but does not attribute easier tuning to community-built tooling.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the pace of an open-source project with a closed version maintained by its creator.

r003.rationale: It does not explain open-source development speed by citing the community's greater aggregate resources.
